dtz.lead: Most adults who apply for Italian citizenship by residence or marriage must show Italian at B1, usually with a certificate from a recognised exam (CILS, CELI, PLIDA or CERT.IT). Here you can read how that works and practise with our own mock.
dtz.practiceHeading: Practise for the B1 language proof
dtz.who.title: Who is this for?
dtz.who.text: For citizenship by residence or marriage, the usual language proof is a certificate at B1 or higher from one of the recognised certifying bodies: CILS, CELI, PLIDA or CERT.IT. Some people are exempt, for example some holders of Italian school or university qualifications. The rules changed in 2025 and can change again, so check the official sources before you book. This is general orientation, not legal advice.
dtz.format.note: This is the structure of our own mock, not of a real exam. For the real parts and timings, see the certifying body of your exam and our CILS B1 practice set. The mock has no speaking part: practise that with our speaking tasks. The extra reading & writing tasks are good for more practice.
dtz.scoring.title: How the B1 certificates are marked
dtz.scoring.text: Each certificate has its own marking rule, published by its certifying body, and the result is a pass or a fail (superato or non superato). In our mock the point bands are our own guide, not an official score.
dtz.set.title: Our B1 mock: listening, reading and writing
dtz.set.text: Our own mock in exam style: listening and reading parts, plus a writing task with a model answer. You can run a clock for each skill. At the end you see your result by part, with our own point bands as a guide. Progress stays saved in the browser.

dtz.mock.text: All four reading tasks as one continuous test at level B1, with an overall result at the end.
dtz.practice.intro: These practice tools train the skills a B1 exam tests.
telc.lead: The CELI certificates of the Università per Stranieri di Perugia, one exam per level. Here you can practise in their style at A2 and B1.
telc.who.title: Who is the CELI for?
telc.who.text: Each CELI level is a separate exam with its own name: CELI 1 is A2, CELI 2 is B1, CELI 3 is B2 and CELI 4 is C1, with CELI Impatto (A1) below and CELI 5 (C2) above; this numbering is to verify. People use it for study, for work and, at the level required, as the language proof for citizenship or the long-term residence permit. Check what your office or university asks for before you book.
telc.sprachbausteine.note: At the higher levels the written exam also tests grammar and vocabulary in context. Check the exact parts for your level on the website of the Università per Stranieri di Perugia (CVCL).
telc.moreLevels.title: How this differs from the real exam
telc.moreLevels.text: Our sets follow the general shape of the CELI levels, but every text and task is our own, and our timings and marks are a guide, not the official ones. The Università per Stranieri di Perugia publishes the current format and sample papers; we do not copy them. Check the details there before you book.

goethe.lead: The CILS (Certificazione di Italiano come Lingua Straniera) is issued by the Università per Stranieri di Siena. It is one of the Italian certificates used for study, work and residence in Italy.

grammatik.artikel.intro: Italian has seven words for “the”: il, lo, l', la, i, gli, le, and four for “a”: un, uno, una, un'. The article matches the noun (masculine or feminine, one or more), and it also depends on the first sound of the noun: il libro, lo studente, l'amico.
grammatik.ja-nein-fragen.intro: A yes/no question uses the same words as a statement. Only the question mark in writing and your voice going up show that it is a question. Put non before the verb to say “not”.
grammatik.w-fragen.intro: The question word comes first, then the verb: Dove abiti? Come si chiama? The main question words are che cosa, chi, dove, quando, come, quanto, perché and quale. Only perché has a written accent.
grammatik.praesens.intro: Italian verbs end in -are, -ere or -ire. Take off the ending and add the one for the person: parlare → parlo, parli, parla. Some -ire verbs add -isc-: finisco, capisci. Use the present for now, for habits and for facts.
grammatik.verb-position-2.intro: Italian uses essere for “to be” in almost every case: Sono Anna. Sono stanca. La farmacia è in via Roma. Stare is for how you are (Come stai? Sto bene) and for “to stay”: Oggi sto a casa.
grammatik.konjugation.intro: The most useful Italian verbs do not follow the rules: andare, fare, stare, venire, dare, uscire, dire, bere, sapere. Learn them whole: vado, faccio, sto, vengo, esco, dico, so.
grammatik.plural.intro: Italian changes the last vowel: -o and -e become -i, -a becomes -e (il libro → i libri, la chiave → le chiavi, la casa → le case). The article and the adjective change too: le case bianche.
grammatik.possessivartikel.intro: Whose is it? Il mio libro, la tua macchina, i suoi figli. Possessives usually come with the article, and they match the thing you have, not the person who has it: la sua casa can be his house or her house. With one family member, drop the article: mia madre, mio fratello.
grammatik.imperativ.intro: Use the imperative to give instructions, advice and invitations. To a friend (tu): Parla più piano! Vieni qui! To someone you address formally (Lei): Mi dica. Si accomodi. The negative with tu uses non + infinitive: Non parlare! With pronouns they attach to the end for tu, noi and voi (Dimmelo! Aspettami!), and go before the verb with Lei (Me lo dica).
grammatik.aduso.intro: Use e (and), o (or), ma (but) and perché (because, and also why) to join words and sentences. Before a word that starts with e-, e often becomes ed. Use anche for “also” and neanche or nemmeno for “not either”.
grammatik.nomen.intro: Every Italian noun is masculine or feminine, even a table or a street. Most nouns ending in -o are masculine (il libro) and most ending in -a are feminine (la casa). Nouns ending in -e can be either. Learn each noun with its article.
grammatik.komposita.intro: To say what is happening right now, use stare + gerundio: Sto lavorando. Stanno mangiando. -are verbs take -ando, -ere and -ire verbs take -endo. For habits and for plans, use the normal present.
grammatik.wortarten.intro: Each word does a job in the sentence. Knowing the job helps you use the word: a noun has a gender, a verb changes for the person, an adjective matches its noun.
grammatik.akkusativ.intro: The direct object is the person or thing the verb acts on. Pronouns: me, te, lo, la, nos, os, los, las. They go before the conjugated verb: Veo a Ana. La veo. A person takes the personal a: Veo a Ana. A thing doesn't: Veo la casa.
grammatik.dativ.intro: Indirect object pronouns say who gets something or who something is said to: mi, ti, gli, le, ci, vi. Gli telefono. Le scrivo. Ci spiega l'orario. They stand before the verb.
grammatik.modalverben.intro: To say what you can, want or must do, use a conjugated verb + an infinitive: Posso aiutare. Voglio riposare. Devo lavorare. Bisogna prenotare. The second verb never changes, and there is no che or di in between.
grammatik.negation.intro: Put non before the verb: Non lavoro. Italian uses double negatives: Non vedo nessuno. Non mangio mai carne. If the negative word comes before the verb, drop non: Nessuno viene. Niente funziona.
grammatik.perfekt.intro: The passato prossimo is the everyday past tense in Italian: Ieri ho lavorato fino alle otto. Stamattina ho chiamato il medico. Most verbs make it with avere + a participle: ho parlato, hai mangiato, ha dormito. Verbs of movement and change use essere instead.
grammatik.satzstellung.intro: Molto, poco, troppo and tanto work in two ways. Before an adjective or after a verb they never change: molto stanco, Lavoro molto. Before a noun they agree with it: molta gente, molti problemi. Abbastanza never changes. Un po' di and del / dei mean “some”.
grammatik.wechselpraepositionen.intro: When a preposition (di, a, da, in, su) meets the article (il, lo, la, l', i, gli, le), the two usually fuse into one word: a + il = al, in + la = nella, di + i = dei. Say Vado al lavoro, not Vado a il lavoro.
grammatik.positionsverben.intro: Some verbs work like piacere: the thing is the subject, and the person takes mi, ti, gli, le, ci, vi. Mi serve un documento. Mi servono due foto. The verb agrees with the thing, not with the person. They are very common in daily life: servire, mancare, bastare, interessare, sembrare, dispiacere, occorrere.
grammatik.praepositionen.intro: Many Italian verbs take one fixed preposition: pensare a, sognare di, dipendere da, credere in, sposarsi con, fidarsi di. It often isn't the one English uses, so learn the verb and the preposition together. With an infinitive you also need the right little word: imparare a, aiutare a, finire di, cercare di.
grammatik.trennbare-verben.intro: To talk about plans and the near future, Italian often uses the plain present with a time word: Domani vado dal medico. In speech you also hear andare a + infinitive: Vado a chiamare il medico. And stare per + infinitive means “about to”: Sto per uscire.
grammatik.zusammengesetzte-verben.intro: Verbs of movement and change use essere in the passato prossimo: Sono andato in banca. Maria è arrivata alle otto. The participle then agrees with the subject, like an adjective: andato, andata, andati, andate.
grammatik.als-oder-wenn.intro: When an indirect and a direct pronoun meet, they join in a fixed order: the indirect one first, and mi, ti, ci, vi become me, te, ce, ve. Il contratto? Me lo ha dato ieri. Gli, le and Lei become glie- and join the second pronoun in one word: Glielo dico domani. Ne joins the same way: Ce ne sono due.
grammatik.n-deklination.intro: Use the imperfetto to talk about how things used to be: habits and descriptions in the past. Da bambino abitavo a Palermo. La casa era piccola. The endings are -avo for -are verbs, -evo for -ere verbs and -ivo for -ire verbs. A few verbs are irregular: essere, fare, dire, bere.
grammatik.genitiv.intro: Many Italian verbs take another verb in the infinitive, often with a fixed little word in between: stare per partire, finire di lavorare, smettere di fumare, cominciare a lavorare, continuare a studiare, tornare a studiare, riuscire a capire, provare a chiamare. The little word (a, di or per) belongs to the verb, so learn them together.
grammatik.adjektivdeklination.intro: Most adjectives go after the noun: una macchina rossa, un medico italiano. A few common ones (bello, buono, brutto, grande, piccolo, nuovo, vecchio) often go before it, and bello, buono and grande then shorten like the article: un buon amico, un bel ragazzo, un gran caldo. Some adjectives change meaning with position: un vecchio amico, un amico vecchio.
grammatik.adjektivdeklination-a2.intro: Add -mente to the feminine form of an adjective to make an adverb: lenta → lentamente, chiara → chiaramente. Adverbs describe a verb: Parli bene. Adjectives describe a noun: È un buon medico.
grammatik.ordinalzahlen.intro: Ordinals up to ten are worth knowing: primo, secondo, terzo… They agree with the noun like any adjective: la seconda strada. Dates use normal numbers, except the first of the month: il 3 maggio, il primo maggio. Floors use ordinals: il secondo piano.
grammatik.zahlen.intro: From 0 to 2000. Italian writes numbers as one word: diciassette, ventidue, centoventi. Before uno and otto the tens lose their last vowel: ventuno, trentotto. Before a noun, uno works like the article: un euro, una casa. Euro never changes: due euro.
grammatik.adjektive-nach-sein.intro: An adjective matches its noun: masculine or feminine, one or more. It usually comes after the noun: una casa bianca, i libri nuovi.
grammatik.gern.intro: In Italian, the thing you like is the subject: mi piace il caffè (coffee pleases me). One thing or an action: mi piace. More than one thing: mi piacciono.
grammatik.praeteritum-sein-haben.intro: Essere (to be) and avere (to have) are the two most important Italian verbs, and both are irregular: sono, sei, è … / ho, hai, ha … Italian uses avere for age, hunger, thirst and cold: Ho trent'anni. Ho fame.
grammatik.berufe-mit-in.intro: Use c'è (one thing) and ci sono (more things) to say that something exists: C'è una farmacia qui vicino. Use è or sono to say where a known thing is: La farmacia è in piazza. Ask with Dov'è…? and point with ecco.
grammatik.konjunktiv2-hoeflich.intro: In Italian you are polite with the right person (tu or Lei), a question and a soft verb form: Può ripetere, per favore? Mi dà un caffè? To ask for something at an office or shop, use vorrei or volevo: Vorrei prenotare una visita.
grammatik.infinitiv-mit-zu.intro: The congiuntivo presente swaps the vowel: -are verbs take -i endings (parli), -ere and -ire verbs take -a endings (scriva, dorma). The three singular persons are identical. Most irregular forms come from the io form of the present: vengo → venga, dico → dica. You will usually see it after che: Voglio che tu venga.
grammatik.praeteritum-plusquamperfekt.in: Use the trapassato prossimo for something that happened before another event in the past. Quando sono arrivato, il treno era già partito. It is the imperfetto of avere or essere plus the participle: avevo mangiato, ero andato. Often with già (already), non… ancora (not yet) and mai (never).
grammatik.indirekte-fragen.intro: To report what someone says, use dice che + a statement: Ana dice che è stanca. To report a yes/no question use chiede se: L'impiegata mi chiede se ho un appuntamento. A question word stays in the sentence: Non so dov'è l'ufficio. Mi può dire quando apre la banca? There is no inversion and no question mark inside the sentence.
grammatik.passiv.intro: Italian has three ways to leave out who does the action. The passive with essere or venire + participle (La domanda è stata presentata. Il modulo viene compilato online.), the si passivante (Si affittano appartamenti. Qui si parla italiano.) and the impersonal si (Si lavora molto qui. Quando si è stanchi, ci si riposa.). In speech and on signs the si form is the most common.
grammatik.passiv-b1.intro: Ci and ne are small words that replace a whole phrase. Ci replaces a place or a thing with a/in: Vai in banca? Sì, ci vado. Ci penso. Ne replaces a quantity or di + something: Quanti figli hai? Ne ho due. Ne parlo con il mio capo. Both stand before the verb. Ci vuole / ci vogliono tell how much time or how many things you need.
grammatik.wortbildung-nomen.intro: The ending of an Italian noun often tells you what it means and its gender. -zione and -tà make feminine nouns: l'informazione, la città. -mento makes masculine ones: il pagamento. -ista, -aio and -iere are people with a job, and -eria is the shop: la pizzeria. -ino, -etto and -ello make things small: un momentino.
grammatik.temporale-praepositionen-b1.in: Italian uses small words to place events in time. Da: something that started in the past and still goes on (Abito qui da tre anni). Per: how long something lasted (Ho lavorato lì per due anni). Fa: how long ago (Sono arrivato tre anni fa). Fra or tra: how long from now (Il corso comincia fra una settimana). Entro: a deadline (entro il 30 giugno). And ci vuole / ci vogliono for the time something takes.
grammatik.infinitiv-ohne-zu.intro: When the subject stays the same, use the infinitive: Voglio partire. Spero di tornare presto. When the subject changes, use che + congiuntivo: Voglio che tu parta. Spero che tu torni presto. For general statements with è importante, bisogna, è meglio, use the infinitive; for one person, che + congiuntivo.
grammatik.funktionen-von-werden.intro: Use the condizionale presente for polite wishes (Vorrei un caffè), polite requests (Potrebbe aiutarmi?), advice (Dovresti parlare con il medico; Io, al tuo posto, andrei in Questura) and imagined situations (Mi piacerebbe vivere al mare). It uses the same stem as the future with the endings -ei, -esti, -ebbe, -emmo, -este, -ebbero: parlerei, avrei, andrei, farei.
grammatik.konjunktiv2.intro: Use the congiuntivo imperfetto when a past verb or a condizionale asks for the congiuntivo: Volevo che venissi. Vorrei che mi chiamassi. Use it with magari for a wish that is unlikely now: Magari avessi più tempo. To make it, take the imperfetto stem (parla-, scrive-, dormi-) and add -ssi, -ssi, -sse, -ssimo, -ste, -ssero.
grammatik.relativpronomen.intro: A relative clause adds information about a noun. Use che for a subject or an object, for people and things: La ragazza che lavora con me è peruviana. After a preposition use cui: La città in cui abito, il medico con cui ho parlato. Chi means whoever (Chi lavora, guadagna) and quello che / ciò che means what (Non capisco quello che dici).
grammatik.irgend.intro: The gerundio replaces a short clause when the subject is the same as in the main clause. Andando a casa, ho visto un incidente (while going home). Essendo stanco, vado a letto (because I am tired). Avendo finito il lavoro, sono uscito (after finishing). Use the simple gerundio for something at the same time, avendo or essendo + participle for something earlier.
grammatik.fokuspartikeln.intro: Italian has one everyday verb for “become”: diventare (È diventato medico. Sono diventata nervosa). Use rimanere or restare for the state you are left in after an event (Sono rimasto senza lavoro), farsi for a gradual change with a few fixed phrases (Si fa tardi), and finire per + infinitive for “end up” (Ha finito per vendere la casa). Many changes of mood have their own reflexive verb: arrabbiarsi, preoccuparsi.
grammatik.negationswoerter.intro: Italian uses the future for a guess about now: Saranno le tre. The futuro anteriore is a guess about something that already happened, even a long time ago: Sarà uscito. Sarà stato stanco. The condizionale passato is for news you cannot confirm: Il ministro si sarebbe dimesso.
grammatik.nomen-verb-verbindungen.intro: Some verbs and nouns go together, and another verb sounds wrong: prendere una decisione, fare la fila, dare una mano, prendere appuntamento, sentire la mancanza di. English often suggests the wrong verb, so learn the pair as one phrase.
grammatik.partizip-als-adjektiv.intro: Use essere + a participle for the state something is in after an action: Il negozio è chiuso. La lettera è scritta. The participle agrees like an adjective: chiuso, chiusa, chiusi, chiuse. Many common participles are irregular: aperto, detto, fatto, messo, rotto, scritto, visto.
grammatik.adjektive-als-nomen.intro: Il + adjective talks about an idea, not a thing or a person: il bello (the nice thing), l'importante (what matters). The adjective doesn't change. Quello che and ciò che mean what, the thing that: Quello che mi serve è tempo. Il bello è che è gratis.
grammatik.zweiteilige-konnektoren.intro: After verbs of opinion, doubt and possibility, standard Italian uses the congiuntivo: Credo che sia vero. Penso che abbiano ragione. Dubito che venga. Può darsi che piova. After verbs of certainty it uses the indicative: So che è vero. È chiaro che hanno ragione. For something already finished, use the congiuntivo passato: Credo che sia arrivato.
grammatik.konditionalsaetze.intro: For something that may really happen, use se + present, and then the present, the future or the imperative: Se piove, resto a casa. Se piove, resterò a casa. Se hai bisogno, chiamami. After a real se there is no congiuntivo. Quando is for things that will certainly happen, se for things that only may happen.
grammatik.konsekutivsaetze.intro: Concession (although): benché, sebbene, nonostante, malgrado + congiuntivo: Benché sia tardi, resto. Nonostante la pioggia, siamo usciti. Consequence (so… that): così / tanto / talmente + aggettivo + che + indicative: Era così stanco che si è addormentato. Result you want to reach: in modo che + congiuntivo: Parla piano in modo che tutti capiscano.
grammatik.zumal-wohingegen.intro: When you report what someone said in the past, the tenses move one step back: Vivo a Torino → Ha detto che viveva a Torino. Ho chiamato → Ha detto che aveva chiamato. Verrò → Ha detto che sarebbe venuto. Orders and requests become di + infinitive (Mi ha detto di aspettare), questions become se or the question word (Mi ha chiesto se avevo il permesso). Time words change too: oggi → quel giorno, domani → il giorno dopo.
grammatik.modalsaetze.intro: For something unlikely or impossible now, use se + congiuntivo imperfetto, and then the condizionale presente: Se avessi più tempo, studierei di più. For advice use Se fossi in te, …. For the past that did not happen use se + congiuntivo trapassato and the condizionale passato: Se l'avessi saputo, sarei venuto. Never put the condizionale after se.
grammatik.reflexive-verben.intro: Many daily-routine verbs need a small pronoun that matches the person: mi alzo, ti lavi, si veste. In the dictionary the verb ends in -si: alzarsi, lavarsi. The pronoun goes before the conjugated verb, and in the passato prossimo the verb uses essere: mi sono alzato.
grammatik.nebensaetze-weil-dass.intro: Give a reason with perché (after the main idea) or siccome (at the start). Give a result with quindi, allora or per questo. To say what someone says or knows, use che: Dice che viene domani. So che è chiuso.
grammatik.komparativ-superlativ.intro: To compare, use più… di, meno… di or tanto… quanto: Questo appartamento è più caro dell'altro. To say “the most”, use il, la, i or le + più: È il più economico. A few words have their own forms: migliore, peggiore, maggiore, minore, and the adverbs meglio and peggio.
grammatik.lokale-praepositionen.intro: To say where something is, use essere + a place word: Le chiavi sono sopra il tavolo. Four small words say the basics: a for cities, in for countries and most buildings, da for someone's place, di for where you come from. Words like accanto a, davanti a and di fronte a give the exact spot.
grammatik.positionsadverbien.intro: Say how often with sempre, spesso, a volte, quasi mai and mai. Use di solito for what you usually do: Di solito mangio alle due. With mai and quasi mai, Italian keeps non before the verb: Non vado mai al cinema.
grammatik.personalpronomen.intro: Io, tu, lui, lei, Lei, noi, voi, loro. The verb ending already shows the person, so Italian often drops the pronoun: Abito a Milano. Use tu with friends and Lei (with a capital L) to be polite.
grammatik.indefinitpronomen.intro: Qualcosa is something, niente (or nulla) is nothing. Qualcuno is someone, nessuno is no one. Qualche and nessun go with a noun: C'è qualche problema? Non c'è nessun problema. Altro means other or more, and ogni means every.
grammatik.temporale-praepositionen.intro: Che ore sono? È l'una. Sono le otto. At what time? Alle otto. Say lunedì for “on Monday”, il lunedì for “on Mondays”, and di mattina for “in the morning”.
grammatik.futur.intro: Use the futuro semplice for plans, predictions and promises: Domani parto. / Domani partirò. Tra dieci anni vivrò in campagna. Ti chiamo appena arrivo → Ti chiamerò appena arriverò. The endings are -ò, -ai, -à, -emo, -ete, -anno, added to the infinitive without the final -e. Many common verbs are irregular: essere → sarò, avere → avrò, andare → andrò, fare → farò.
grammatik.temporale-nebensaetze.intro: After quando, appena, dopo che, mentre and finché Italian uses the indicative: Quando ho tempo, leggo. Appena arrivo, ti chiamo. For future events the futuro is common: Quando arriverò, ti chiamerò. Before: prima di + infinitive when the subject is the same (Prima di partire, chiamo il medico), prima che + congiuntivo when it changes (Chiamami prima che tu parta).
grammatik.da-wo-woerter.intro: After a preposition, Italian uses me and te, not io and tu: per me, con te, da me. The other persons stay the same: con lui, per lei, senza di noi, da loro. The same forms stress a person: A me piace, a lui no. Chiama me, non lui.
grammatik.lassen.intro: Fare + infinitive says that someone else does the action for you, or that you make someone do it: Faccio riparare la macchina (I have the car repaired). Mi faccio tagliare i capelli. Fammi vedere. Lasciare + infinitive means to let someone do something: Lasciami parlare. Il medico non lascia uscire nessuno.
grammatik.modalpartikeln.intro: Small words like allora, dunque, cioè, insomma, ecco, magari, mica, mah and boh keep a conversation going: they start, conclude, rephrase, hesitate, hand over or soften. They belong to speech and informal messages, not to a formal email or a letter to an office.
grammatik.adjektive-mit-praepositionen.i: Many adjectives take a fixed preposition: stufo di, capace di, contento di, interessato a, preoccupato per, abituato a. Add a noun, an infinitive for the same person, or che + congiuntivo for another person.
grammatik.konnektoren-grund-gegengrund.i: Linkers connect your ideas and make your Italian sound organised. Anche se (although) is followed by the indicative: Anche se sono stanco, vado a lavorare. Contrast: però, tuttavia, invece. Addition: inoltre. Result: quindi, dunque. Lavora moltissimo; tuttavia guadagna poco. Ho la febbre, quindi resto a casa.
grammatik.finalsaetze.intro: To say what you do something for, use per + infinitive when the subject stays the same: Studio per trovare lavoro. When another person does the second action, use perché or affinché + congiuntivo: Parlo piano perché tu mi capisca. Perché with the indicative means because: Resto a casa perché piove.
grammatik.zustandspassiv.intro: In one story you use two past tenses. The imperfetto sets the scene: weather, time, age, feelings, habits (Pioveva, ero stanco). The passato prossimo tells the events that happen, one after the other (Sono rimasto a casa, ho chiamato il medico). Ieri pioveva e sono rimasto a casa.
grammatik.relativsaetze-was-wo.intro: Use the indicative for something you know exists, and the congiuntivo for something unknown or that does not exist: Conosco una persona che parla inglese. Cerco una persona che parli inglese. A preposition goes first: la casa in cui abito, la persona con cui ho parlato, l'azienda per la quale lavoro.
grammatik.konjunktiv-1.intro: The tense of the main verb decides the tense of the congiuntivo. Present main verb: Penso che sia a casa. Penso che sia partito. Past main verb or condizionale: Pensavo che fosse a casa. Pensavo che fosse partito. The congiuntivo trapassato (avesse, fosse + participle) says that the action was already finished.
grammatik.subjektive-modalverben.intro: The passato remoto is the past tense of novels, history books and biographies: Dante nacque a Firenze. Il re morì in battaglia. In the south it is also spoken. You need to recognise it fluently, and you can use it for the third person: fu, ebbe, fece, disse, andò, venne, vide. In everyday speech elsewhere, the passato prossimo takes its place.
grammatik.passiversatz.intro: Italian has other ways to set a condition besides se. Qualora is a formal se: Qualora Lei abbia bisogno, ci contatti. Purché and a patto che mean “as long as”. A meno che non means “unless”. Nel caso in cui and in caso di name the case. A gerund does it in one word: Volendo, puoi venire.
grammatik.partizipialattribute.intro: Formal Italian has more relatives than che. Il quale, la quale, i quali, le quali follow a preposition or a comma and make the reference clear: il motivo per il quale. Cui comes after a preposition: la persona a cui scrivo. Il cui, la cui mean “whose”. Il che refers to a whole idea. And the verb after che can be in the congiuntivo: Cerco una persona che sappia l'inglese.
grammatik.nominalisierung.intro: Formal and administrative Italian often turns a verb into a noun: presentare → la presentazione, pagare → il pagamento, scadere → la scadenza. A noun phrase such as la presentazione della domanda says in one group what a clause says in several words. You read it every day in forms, notices and contracts. Learn the suffixes and the prepositions that go with them.
grammatik.nominale-praepositionen.intro: Letters, reports, notices and contracts link ideas with formal words. A causa di and a seguito di give a cause, in virtù di and ai sensi di give a legal basis, tuttavia and nondimeno mark a contrast, pertanto marks a consequence, in merito a opens a reference. Learn which ones take a noun and which ones take a clause.
grammatik.irreale-vergleiche.intro: Come se compares something with a situation that isn't real. Same time: congiuntivo imperfetto, Parla come se sapesse tutto. Earlier: congiuntivo trapassato, Fa come se non fosse successo niente. The same two forms build the unreal past: Se l'avessi saputo, sarei venuto. And they can be mixed: Se avessi studiato di più, ora avrei un lavoro migliore.
grammatik.futur-2.intro: A clause without a conjugated verb says the same thing in fewer words. The participio assoluto: Finita la riunione, siamo usciti. The gerundio: Vedendo che non rispondeva, l'ho richiamato. Dopo aver + participle: Dopo aver mangiato, siamo usciti. Pur essendo stanca, ha continuato. These forms belong to careful writing and formal speech.
grammatik.es-korrelat.intro: A cleft sentence puts the spotlight on one part of the message. Use essere + the part in focus + che: È Anna che ha chiamato. È qui che abito. Or start with what you want to explain: Quello che mi serve è tempo. Dislocation does a similar job in speech: Il libro, l'ho già letto.
grammatik.textkohaerenz.intro: A good text holds together. Reference words point back: ciò, quest'ultimo, il primo … il secondo, tale, suddetto. The neutral lo stands for a quality or a whole idea: Sei medico? Sì, lo sono. Ellipsis leaves out what is clear: the subject, a repeated noun. Linkers (infatti, anzi, invece, inoltre) organise the argument, and register (tu or Lei, ciò or questo) fits the reader.
grammatik.verbpraefixe.intro: A prefix changes a word's meaning. Ri- repeats: rifare. In- and dis- deny: infelice, disonesto. Pre- comes before: prevedere. Sotto- and sovra- go under or over: sottovalutare, sovraccarico. Contro- and anti- go against: controproposta, antifurto. Endings such as -ino, -one and -accio add size or attitude: tavolino, portone, tempaccio. Learn the pattern and you guess the meaning of new words.
grammatik.nutzen-benutzen.intro: Some Italian verbs look alike in English and are easy to mix up. Sapere is for facts and skills (So dov'è il Comune. So nuotare.), conoscere for people and places (Conosco Luca. Conosci Roma?). Portare is to carry, bring or wear, prendere is to take, catch or have. Venire is to come towards the person you talk to (Vieni da me?), andare is to go away from here. Partire, uscire and lasciare are three different kinds of leaving.
grammatik.verben-als-nomen.intro: Use the congiuntivo after che when you express a wish, a need, a hope, a feeling or an opinion: Voglio che tu venga. Spero che sia facile. Mi dispiace che tu stia male. Penso che sia giusto. After verbs of knowing or saying a fact (so che, vedo che, dico che) Italian uses the indicative.
grammatik.artikel-oder-nicht.intro: Italian uses il, la, i, gli, le for things in general with piacere: Mi piace il caffè. With an indefinite amount, the plain noun is normal: Bevo acqua. Non ho tempo. No article for jobs and languages: Sono medico. Parlo italiano. No article after in with most countries: Vado in Italia.
grammatik.welcher-dieser.intro: This one, that one: questo is near you (qui), quello is far from you (lì). Both match the noun: questa casa, questi libri. Before a noun, quello changes like the article: quel libro, quello zaino, quell'ufficio, quei libri.
grammatik.artikel-oder-nicht.brief:
Why “Mi piace il caffè” but “Bevo acqua”? Why “Sono medico” with no article?

  • —No article: jobs, languages, an amount of something, in + most countries (in Italia).
  • un, unaOne of many, or a new thing: C'è una farmacia.
  • il, laThe one we both know, things in general with piacere, “every Monday” (il lunedì).

home.mock.hint.0: a + il = al: supermercato is masculine and starts with s + vowel, so il, not lo.
home.mock.hint.1: piacere agrees with what is liked — here a plural.
home.mock.hint.2: One thing exists somewhere: use c'è.
home.mock.hint.4: A wish about someone else: che + congiuntivo.
home.mock.hint.5: An unreal condition with se: congiuntivo imperfetto.
home.mock.pronNote.0: The stress falls on the second syllable: se-CON-do me.
home.mock.pronNote.1: A double consonant is held longer. pala (shovel) and palla (ball) are different words.
home.mock.pronNote.2: z sounds like “ts” here, and the final e is clearly spoken: GRA-tsie.
home.mock.pronNote.3: rr is a rolled trill, held longer than a single r: BIR-ra.
home.mock.pronNote.4: ch before e and i sounds like k — the h is silent: ke KO-sa.

kultur.sourcingNote:
Every topic here is factual knowledge: publicly checkable facts about rules, institutions and procedures in Italy (laws, who is responsible, what you do), written by icanspeak Italian from official sources such as gazzettaufficiale.it, the portals of the ministries and of INPS, and the pages of the Comuni. Italy comes first; Italian in Switzerland, San Marino and the world follows.
What is deliberately NOT here: claims about “the Italian character”. Nothing is claimed about people; rules, figures and responsibilities are, and where practice differs by region, Comune or person, the topic says so.
Rules and figures change. A figure carries its date; if in doubt, the official source is right, not this page. This is general orientation, not legal advice.

akk.regel.intro: The direct object is the person or thing the verb acts on: Vedo Anna. Vedo la casa. There is no a before a person (Spanish speakers, careful): Vedo Anna, not Vedo a Anna. The pronoun goes before the conjugated verb: La vedo.
akk.regel.example: Common mistake: Vedo la. → La vedo. With an infinitive it goes on the end: Voglio vederla. In the passato prossimo, lo and la become l' and the participle agrees: L'ho vista ieri. Li ho chiamati.

sets.prog.title: Your progress
sprechen.check.a1-sich-vorstellen.1: Full sentences, not a list: “Ho 29 anni.”, not just “29”. Age goes with avere, not essere. A job takes no article after essere: “Sono elettricista.” Or use fare: “Faccio l'elettricista.”
sprechen.check.a1-sich-vorstellen.2: End with your free time: it is a natural next question.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-bahnhof.0: “Nella foto vedo …” is the easiest way to start. No little word is needed before the person or thing: vedo una donna, vedo un treno.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-bahnhof.1: “Forse …” and “probabilmente …” let you guess without being sure.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-bahnhof.2: The last sentence is about you: that is a natural next question.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-kueche.0: First count (“due persone”), then say the place, then the action. This order always works.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-kueche.1: For what is happening now, use stare + -ando or -endo: sta cucinando, sta mangiando. The simple present (cucina) is fine too.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-supermarkt.0: Frutta and verdura are singular in Italian: compro frutta e verdura. But le mele and le banane are plural.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-supermarkt.1: “alla cassa”, “con la carta”, “in contanti”: learn the little word with the phrase.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-supermarkt.2: A time phrase at the end (“il sabato”, “una volta a settimana”) sounds practised straight away.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-spielplatz.0: Two people, two descriptions: first the boy, then the girl.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-spielplatz.1: One sentence about the weather, with fare: fa bel tempo, fa caldo. Or with c'è: c'è il sole.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-spielplatz.2: “perché” joins your reason to your sentence: mi piace il parco perché è tranquillo. Mind the accent: perché.
sprechen.check.a2-bild-nachbarschaftsfes: Say what is in primo piano and sullo sfondo: that is the step from A1 to A2.
A guess with a reason: “Secondo me è …, perché …”
End with a comparison with your own life or country. At A2 a comparison like this is a natural last step.
sprechen.check.a2-bild-wartezimmer.0: Say how someone feels and why: “Sembra preoccupata. Forse …” Pictures with people often invite this question.
sprechen.check.a2-bild-wartezimmer.1: Say what you can and can't see: “Vediamo solo il suo braccio.”
sprechen.check.a2-bild-wartezimmer.2: A real detail from your own life (“a volte aspetto una settimana”) is worth more than a general sentence.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-bewerbungsgesprae: Use place words to organise what you say: a sinistra, a destra, di fronte a, sullo sfondo.
Show that a guess is a guess (“Direi che …”, “potrebbe essere …”) and give a reason.
The part in the past is expected at B1: the passato prossimo for the event (“ho fatto”), the imperfetto for how you felt (“ero”).
One sentence with “Secondo me”: giving your opinion is the real B1 part.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-werkstatt.0: “Suppongo che …, perché …” joins a guess and a reason in one sentence. After “suppongo che” the subjunctive follows: “stia insegnando”.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-werkstatt.1: Explain a word (apprendistato) instead of just saying it.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-werkstatt.2: The “perché?” question gets a real answer with “perché” or “Una ragione potrebbe essere che …”.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-buergeramt.0: Show how you know something: “Si capisce che …, perché …”
sprechen.check.b1-bild-buergeramt.1: Give a real example from your own life instead of a general complaint.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-buergeramt.2: “Adesso …” shows how things have changed, which is a useful B1 skill.
You react to the other person instead of working through your own list.
Disagree politely at least once: that is what the task tests.
At the end you clearly agree on every point.
Polite forms with the conditional: proporrei, sceglierei, potremmo …? Colleagues use tu; with a boss you hardly know, switch to Lei.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wochenmarkt.0: The description is short. At B2 it is the way in, not the task.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wochenmarkt.1: Both sides are there, with the linking words for them: un vantaggio evidente, d'altra parte, non bisogna dimenticare.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wochenmarkt.2: Saying “non è solo …, ma anche …” shows you have really thought the question through.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wochenmarkt.3: The personal ending is honest rather than perfect: that is harder to say and sounds more mature.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-videokonferenz.0: Something you notice in the picture (“Quello che mi colpisce è che …”) supports your argument, not just general knowledge.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-videokonferenz.1: The objection to your own view is there (“Alcuni diranno che …”) and you answer it.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-videokonferenz.2: The difference between “giorni in ufficio per tutta la squadra” and “una regola per ogni persona” is a fine distinction. That is exactly what separates B2 from B1.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-baustelle-innenst: A detail from the picture (the flats right next to the site) becomes part of the argument, not just a description.
“La vera questione non è se …, ma come …” moves the discussion on: a strong B2 phrase.
The opinion ends with conditions, not a simple yes or no. That is more balanced and easier to defend.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wertstoffhof.0: A system is explained, not just judged.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wertstoffhof.1: The counter-argument and your answer to it are both there.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wertstoffhof.2: “Riciclare limita il danno; non risolve il problema”: a short, sharp sentence at the end stays with the listener.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wertstoffhof.3: The comparison with your own country doesn't judge; it describes a difference.

ac.find.h: The h in “{word}” is silent. Start straight on the next vowel.
ac.find.doppie: “{word}” has a double consonant: hold it about twice as long, and keep the vowel before it short.
ac.find.vocali: “{word}”: keep every vowel short and clear, the last one too. No glide, no weak “uh”.
ac.find.eo: In “{word}” listen to the stressed e or o: open or closed. è is open, perché is closed.
ac.find.r: “{word}” has r: a single r is one quick tap of the tongue tip, rr and a first r are several. caro is not carro.
ac.find.cg: “{word}”: ce, ci and ge, gi are soft (like “church”, “jam”); che, chi and ghe, ghi are hard: k and g.
ac.find.sc: “{word}”: sce and sci are like sh in “ship”; sche and schi are s + k.
ac.find.gngl: “{word}” has gn or gli: one sound, with the middle of your tongue against the roof of your mouth. Not g + n, not g + l.
ac.find.z: “{word}” has z: a ts or a dz, the tongue at your teeth with a hiss. Not a buzz, not th.
ac.find.s: In “{word}”, s before b, d, g, l, m, n, r or v is voiced, like z in “zoo”.
ac.find.bv: “{word}”: b closes both lips; v touches the top teeth to your lower lip. They are two different sounds.
ac.find.qu: “{word}” has qu: say k + w, you hear the u.
ac.find.stsp: “{word}” starts with s + a consonant: start straight on a clean s, with no vowel in front.
ac.find.tidi: “{word}”: t and d stay plain before i, no “ch” and no “j”.
ac.find.betonung: “{word}”: one syllable is strong. Listen for it again, and follow the written accent if there is one.

mhelp.kultur.what: Here you learn how everyday life in Italy works: meal times, the Comune, the medico di base, public holidays and much more.
mhelp.kultur.s1: Pick a topic at your level (A1, A2 …).
mhelp.kultur.s2: Read the short text and look at the examples.
mhelp.kultur.s3: Then answer the quiz questions. That way you remember what matters.
mhelp.wortgeschichte.what: Etymology is the story of a word: where it comes from, how it used to sound and what it used to mean. Italian words come from Latin, Greek, Germanic languages, Arabic and more, so some may be related to words in your language.
mhelp.wortgeschichte.s1: “The root” shows the oldest form of the word we know.
mhelp.wortgeschichte.s2: Read the family tree from the bottom up: from the root to the words of today.
mhelp.wortgeschichte.s3: “Tracing it in other languages” shows the word in your language. Tip: tap the speaker to hear the word.
mhelp.grammatik.what: Every grammar topic, sorted by level — each with a rule and exercises.
mhelp.grammatik.s1: Choose your level and a topic, or follow the guided path to go step by step in the right order.
mhelp.grammatik.s2: Read the rule first, then do the exercises.
mhelp.grammatik.s3: Your results are saved. You can see them under „Mein Fortschritt“.
mhelp.hoeren.what: Practise listening: announcements, phone calls, conversations and radio pieces from A1 to B2.
mhelp.hoeren.s1: Choose a text at your level.
mhelp.hoeren.s2: Listen as often as you like — slower, too.
mhelp.hoeren.s3: Answer the questions. Afterwards the transcript helps you.
mhelp.lesen.what: Practise reading with real kinds of text: signs, adverts, emails and articles.

mhelp.lesen.s2: Read the text calmly. There is no rush.
mhelp.lesen.s3: Answer the questions and read the explanation for each answer.
mhelp.sprechen.what: Practise speaking as in the exam: describe pictures, introduce yourself, plan together, discuss.

sprachen.benrath.text: Italian grew out of the Tuscan of Florence and became the common language of Italy. Millions of Italians emigrated, so large Italian-speaking communities live in the Americas, Australia and Europe. Pick a country to see how Italian is used there.
sprachen.count.native: people have Italian as their first language
sprachen.count.dialect: people can hold a conversation in Italian
sprachen.c.ITA: The home of Italian. Standard Italian is the language of school, work, offices and television, but many people also speak a regional language or dialect at home, and regional Italian sounds different from north to south (see the accents map). Some regions have recognised minority languages, such as German in South Tyrol and French in the Aosta Valley.
sprachen.c.SMR: A small republic inside Italy. Italian is the official language, used in offices and schools. The local speech is close to the dialects of Romagna.
sprachen.c.VAT: Italian is the official language of the Vatican City State, the smallest state in the world. Latin is used for some church documents, and many other languages are heard from visitors and from the Church's staff.
sprachen.c.CHE: Italian is one of Switzerland's four national languages, beside German, French and Romansh. It is the main language of Ticino and of a few southern valleys of Graubünden. Swiss Italian is standard Italian with some local words (see the accents map).
sprachen.c.SVN: Slovene is the official language, and Italian is co-official in the coastal municipalities where an Italian community lives (Koper, Izola, Piran). There you find bilingual signs and Italian-language schools.
sprachen.c.HRV: Croatian is the official language. Italian has official status beside it in some local units of Istria County, where an Italian community lives and has its own schools and clubs.
sprachen.c.ARG: A very large share of Argentinians has Italian ancestry. The big waves of immigration from the late 19th century shaped Buenos Aires: Rioplatense Spanish sounds Italian in its melody and has many words from Italian dialects.
sprachen.c.BRA: Millions of Brazilians descend from Italian immigrants, above all in São Paulo and in the south. In Rio Grande do Sul and Santa Catarina, Talian, a language based on Venetian, is still spoken and is recognised as part of the cultural heritage.
sprachen.c.URY: Many Uruguayans have Italian roots, and Italian words are part of everyday Rioplatense Spanish. You find Italian associations and courses in Montevideo.
sprachen.c.VEN: A large Italian community arrived after the Second World War. Many families still use Italian or a regional language at home, and many Venezuelans of Italian descent have moved to Italy in recent years.
sprachen.c.USA: One of the largest Italian-heritage populations in the world. Most families speak English now, but Italian is taught in schools and spoken by older people, often in the regional languages of the south that their ancestors brought.
sprachen.c.CAN: Large Italian communities live in Toronto and Montreal, built by immigration after the Second World War. Italian is widely heard in the old Italian neighbourhoods and is offered in some schools.
sprachen.c.AUS: Italians were one of the largest groups of migrants after the Second World War, above all in Melbourne and Sydney. Italian is one of the most common languages spoken at home, though many speakers are now older.
sprachen.c.DEU: Many Italians moved to Germany for work from the 1950s on. Italian is heard in families, restaurants and associations in cities such as Stuttgart, Munich and Wolfsburg.
sprachen.c.FRA: A long history of Italian immigration. In Nice and in Corsica, which were close to Italian for centuries, Italian words and family names are still common.
sprachen.c.MLT: Italian was an official language of Malta until 1934. Many Maltese still understand it, partly thanks to Italian television, and Maltese has many words from Italian and Sicilian.
sprachen.c.ALB: Italian television reached Albania in the 1980s and 1990s, and many Albanians learned the language from it. It is widely understood, and many Albanians have lived or worked in Italy.
sprachen.m.eritrea: A former Italian colony until 1941. Older people in Asmara still speak Italian, and an Italian school still exists there, but the language is fading.
sprachen.tree.title: The language family
sprachen.tree.lead: Italian is a Romance language: it grew out of the Latin spoken in Roman Italy. Romance belongs to the large Indo-European family, so many languages from Iceland to India share distant roots with it.
sprachen.tree.otherLead: These languages are not related to Italian, though several have lived beside it for centuries. That doesn't make Italian harder: it just means you learn words fresh rather than recognising them.
sprachen.tree.names: Language names are given in English. The tree is simplified: how exactly the Romance languages group together is debated.
sprachen.cmp.title: How close is your language?
sprachen.cmp.lead: Pick your first language. Eight basic words show how much you already bring with you.
sprachen.cmp.fehler: Typical mistakes with this first language
sprachen.cmp.englisch: English is Germanic, but it took thousands of words from French and Latin, so you can already read a lot of Italian: animale, importante, possibile. Watch out for false friends: camera means room, not camera, and parenti means relatives, not parents.
sprachen.cmp.deutsch: German is Germanic, a distant relative of Italian: Mutter – madre, drei – tre. You already know grammatical gender and verb endings, which helps. Italian has only two genders and no noun cases, but it has more past tenses, and a subjunctive you will use every day.
sprachen.cmp.franzoesisch: French is a close relative. Most grammar will feel familiar: articles, gender, passé composé and imparfait (passato prossimo and imperfetto), the subjunctive. The new parts are the double consonants, the clear vowels, and the fact that every letter is pronounced. Watch out: parenti means relatives, not parents.
sprachen.cmp.portugiesisch: A close relative of Italian: you can understand a lot from day one, so the danger is false friends. Esquisito means strange in Portuguese, but squisito means delicious in Italian. Italian also has no nasal vowels, and its double consonants matter: pala and palla are different words.
sprachen.cmp.rumaenisch: Romanian is also Romance, although it has been surrounded by Slavic languages for centuries: noapte – notte, apă – acqua. Italian nouns have no cases, and the article goes before the noun: la casa, not casa. Many Romanians live in Italy, so you may meet plenty of people who have made the same journey.
sprachen.cmp.arabisch: Arabic belongs to the Afro-Asiatic family and is not related to Italian. But Italian has many Arabic words: zucchero (sukkar), arancia, magazzino, algebra. Italian spelling shows how a word is said, so reading aloud is quite easy.
sprachen.cmp.russisch: Russian is Slavic, another branch of the same family: мать – madre, три – tre. Italian nouns have no cases, but there are articles (il, la), which Russian doesn't have. The rolled r will come easily to you.
sprachen.cmp.ukrainisch: Ukrainian is Slavic and distantly related to Italian: ніч – notte, три – tre. Italian nouns have no cases, so word order and prepositions do that job, and articles (il, la) are new. The rolled r will come easily to you.
sprachen.cmp.chinesisch: Chinese is Sino-Tibetan and not related to Italian. Good news: Italian has no tones, and its spelling tells you how to say each word. The big new step is verbs: every person and tense has its own ending.
sprachen.cmp.spanisch: Spanish is a close relative of Italian, with the same clear vowels and similar verbs. Watch out for false friends: burro is a donkey in Spanish, but burro means butter in Italian, and salir means to go out, while salire means to climb. Italian also has double consonants that change the meaning.
sprachen.cmp.note: Being related helps with vocabulary. For grammar and pronunciation, practice is what counts.
sprachen.dec.title: English → Italian: the word decoder
sprachen.dec.lead: English took thousands of words from Latin and French, and Italian grew out of Latin. So many long English words are really Italian words in disguise. If you know English, these patterns let you guess a lot of Italian.
sprachen.dec.step1: At the top is a pattern: English on the left, Italian on the right.
sprachen.dec.step2: Below are examples: English word → Italian word.
sprachen.dec.step3: Try it with a word you know: swap the pattern and say it. Often you get a real Italian word, and people will understand you.
sprachen.dec.note: They're rules of thumb: not every word fits, and accents and double consonants have to be learned (università, elettrico, differenza). Watch out for false friends: attualmente means at present, not actually; sensibile means sensitive; parenti means relatives, not parents; and camera means room.
sprachen.dec.quiz: Try it yourself: what is it in Italian?

dialekte.title: Regional varieties of Italian and Italy's other languages
dialekte.lead: From the Alps to Sicily: how Italian sounds in different parts of Italy, which other languages you will meet there, and how Swiss Italian differs. Pick a region for examples and typical words.
dialekte.map.title: The accent map
dialekte.map.lead: The colours show the big groups of regional Italian. The dots are well-known city accents and the other languages of Italy. Click an area or a dot to read about it.
dialekte.map.empty: Click a region or a dot on the map.
dialekte.map.wordNote: Simplified: in many places you hear several forms, and the standard word is understood everywhere. To verify against a regional atlas.
dialekte.group.nord.text: The s between vowels is voiced, as in casa with /z/. Double consonants are often shorter than in the standard, and in speech people use the passato prossimo rather than the passato remoto.
dialekte.group.centro.text: Tuscan is the base of standard Italian, so its sounds are close to what this course teaches, but Tuscany has its own gorgia (la casa becomes la hasa). Around Rome the s in casa is voiceless and a consonant after some short words is doubled (a ccasa).
dialekte.group.sud.text: Consonants are strong and long, the passato remoto is common in speech, and stare often replaces essere. Words like mo' (now) and assai (very) are everywhere.
dialekte.group.isole.text: Both islands have strong local languages under their Italian. In Sicily you hear the passato remoto and a sing-song melody; in Sardinia a clear, even rhythm, with Sardinian words such as ajò.
dialekte.r.nordovest: Piedmont, Lombardy, Liguria and the Aosta Valley share the sound of the north: the voiced s in casa, shorter double consonants and a rather flat melody. Each area adds words of its own, such as michetta in Milan and neh at the end of a question in Piedmont. French is also official in the Aosta Valley.
dialekte.r.nordest: The Veneto, Trentino-Alto Adige and Friuli-Venezia Giulia. The accent is melodic, and many people in the Veneto speak Venetian at home. South Tyrol is mostly German-speaking, with German and Italian both official; Friulian is spoken in Friuli, and Slovene around Trieste.
dialekte.r.emilia: Bologna, Modena and Parma sound alike, while Romagna has a melody of its own. Emilian and Romagnol dialects are still heard. The filler mo and food words such as piada and crescentina turn up in everyday Italian.
dialekte.r.toscana: Tuscan is closest to standard Italian in vocabulary and grammar, because the standard grew out of the Florentine of the Middle Ages. Typical are the gorgia toscana (c between vowels becomes a breath: la hasa), babbo for dad, and repeating the subject pronoun: icché tu fai?
dialekte.r.marcheumbria: Marche and Umbria sit between the north and the south, with a gentle accent. The north of the Marche is close to Romagna, the south of Umbria closer to Rome. Food words such as crescia and torta al testo are everyday words here.
dialekte.r.lazio: The speech of Rome (romanesco) colours the Italian of the whole region and is known across Italy from films and television. Typical are the exclamations aò and daje, nun for non, doubled consonants across words (a ccasa) and quick, relaxed speech.
dialekte.r.abruzzo: Abruzzo and Molise sound southern: strong consonants, mo' for adesso and mannaggia. Food names such as arrosticini and scrippelle come from the local dialects. A few villages in Molise speak Croatian or Albanian.
dialekte.r.campania: Naples has the most famous accent of the south, and Neapolitan reaches the whole of Italy through songs, theatre and film. In local Italian you hear uè and guagliò, doubled consonants, stare for essere (sto a casa) and final vowels that fade.
dialekte.r.puglia: Bari and the north of Apulia sound different from Salento in the south, which has its own melody and words such as sciamu. Many people mix Italian with the local dialect, and unstressed vowels at the end of words are weak.
dialekte.r.calabria: A clear, strong southern accent with doubled consonants, and assai for molto. Calabrian and Basilicata food has given Italian words that you see on menus ('nduja, peperoni cruschi). A few villages speak Albanian or Greek.
dialekte.r.sicilia: Sicilian is a language of its own, and Italian in Sicily has its melody, long consonants and many Sicilian words. The passato remoto is used in speech, and some names differ from place to place: arancina in Palermo, arancino in Catania. Do not copy strong words: listen first.
dialekte.r.sardegna: Sardinian is very different from Italian, so Italian in Sardinia often has a clear, even rhythm and sometimes sounds that follow Sardinian. Ajò and eja are heard in everyday Italian. Alghero is a Catalan-speaking town.
dialekte.m.milano: Milan speech is quick and businesslike, with the flat northern melody. Milan gave Italy habits such as the aperitivo, and the word dai, used to push someone along or to comfort them, is heard everywhere in the north.
dialekte.m.firenze: Florentine is the base of standard Italian, yet Florence speakers have the gorgia toscana, icché for che cosa and the doubled subject pronoun (tu fai). Visitors often notice the breathy h for c.
dialekte.m.roma: Rome mixes the Italian of the whole country with its own romanesco. Romanesco words and exclamations (aò, daje, anvedi) are known across Italy thanks to films. You need not copy the strongest ones, but expect to hear them.
dialekte.m.lugano: Swiss Italian is standard Italian with some words from Swiss German and French: natel for the mobile phone (cellulare in Italy), cassa malati for the health insurance fund. At home, many Ticino speakers use a local dialect of the Lombard group.
dialekte.m.sardo: Sardinian is a Romance language of its own, with several varieties, and Italian law recognises it. It is not a dialect of Italian. Many people use it with family and friends, and you see it on bilingual signs.
dialekte.m.friulano: Friulian is a Romance language spoken by hundreds of thousands of people in Friuli, and Italian law recognises it. You hear it in shops and families and see it on road signs. Mandi serves as hello and as goodbye.
dialekte.m.ladino: Ladin is a Romance language of the Dolomite valleys, spoken by a few tens of thousands of people. In the Ladin valleys of South Tyrol it is used beside Italian and German, and schools there teach in all three.
dialekte.m.napoletano: Neapolitan is spoken by millions of people in Naples and Campania, with a rich tradition of songs, theatre and film. Related varieties are spoken in much of the south. For most people it lives beside Italian rather than instead of it.
dialekte.m.siciliano: Sicilian has a long literary history, from the court poets of the 13th century, and is spoken across Sicily. It has given Italian a number of food words. For most Sicilians it lives beside Italian.
dialekte.m.tedesco: In South Tyrol (Alto Adige) German is the first language of most people, and it is co-official with Italian. Offices, schools and signs are in both languages. You will hear Servus and Grüß Gott next to buongiorno.
dialekte.m.francese: French is co-official in the Aosta Valley, and Franco-Provençal is the traditional home language. Signs and offices use Italian and French, and children learn both at school.
dialekte.m.sloveno: Slovene is spoken by the Slovene minority around Trieste and Gorizia. The law protects it, and there are Slovene-language schools and bilingual signs in some areas.
dialekte.m.arberesh: Arbëreshë is an old form of Albanian that came to Italy with refugees in the 15th century. It is spoken in dozens of villages in the south and in Sicily, and it is protected by law.
dialekte.m.algherese: The Catalan of Alghero (alguerès) goes back to a Catalan-Aragonese settlement of the 14th century. It is still spoken and taught in some schools, and Italian is used there every day too.
dialekte.m.veneto: Venetian was the language of the Republic of Venice and is spoken in the whole of the Veneto. Many families still use it at home, and the Veneto Region has promoted it; it is not recognised as a minority language at national level.
dialekte.lines.title: Two lines across Italy
dialekte.lines.lead: Two differences explain much of what you hear. The lines on the map show roughly where they run. Real borders are wide and blurred, and younger speakers often sound different from older ones.
dialekte.lines.benrath.title: The s line: casa with /z/ | casa with /s/
dialekte.lines.benrath.text: In the north and in Tuscany, the s between two vowels is usually voiced, like z in zoo (casa, rosa). From Umbria and Lazio southwards it is usually voiceless, like s in sun. Both are heard and understood everywhere, and the standard allows both.
dialekte.lines.speyer.title: The past tense line: passato prossimo | passato remoto
dialekte.lines.speyer.text: In the north, people mostly say ho mangiato and use the passato remoto (mangiai) only in writing. In Tuscany and much of the south it is also common in speech, above all in Sicily. Learners are fine with the passato prossimo everywhere.
dialekte.lines.note: Simplified: inside every group there are many local accents, and the same person may speak differently at work and at home. Spelling never changes: everyone writes casa, cena and città.
dialekte.world.title: Italian beyond Italy
dialekte.world.lead: This course teaches standard Italian, but your neighbours, colleagues and favourite series may sound different. The varieties of Italian in Switzerland, San Marino and the communities abroad all understand each other and share one spelling. Words can differ, too: the same thing may have a regional name.
dialekte.w.svizzera: Ticino and the southern valleys of Graubünden use standard Italian at school, in offices and in the media, with Swiss words and a slightly slower melody. Loanwords from Swiss German and French appear in daily life.
dialekte.w.istria: In Slovene and Croatian Istria, the Italian community speaks Italian and, in families, an old Istrian variety close to Venetian. You see bilingual signs, and Italian-language schools and community clubs beside them.
dialekte.w.argentina: Rioplatense Spanish took its melody and many words from the Italian dialects of the immigrants: laburo (from lavoro) and chau (from ciao) are everyday Spanish here. Standard Italian is taught and used in clubs.
dialekte.w.brasile: In the south of Brazil, descendants of immigrants from the Veneto speak Talian, a language based on Venetian. It is recognised as part of Brazil's cultural heritage. It differs from the Italian you learn here, but a speaker of Venetian understands a good part of it.
dialekte.w.usa: The Italian of many American families comes from the dialects their ancestors spoke, mostly from the south, so some words differ from standard Italian: pasta fazool for pasta e fagioli, gabagool for capocollo. Standard Italian is taught in schools and universities.
dialekte.learn.title: Do I have to learn an accent?
dialekte.learn.text: No. Use the standard Italian you learn here: it is understood everywhere and works in every exam, office and workplace. Regional sounds are not mistakes, so there is no need to correct people or to change how you speak. If you live in Naples or Turin, train your ear first. The local words will follow by themselves.

dialekte.src.text: A simplified overview following the usual descriptions of the varieties of Italian (for example Treccani and the Accademia della Crusca). Real accent borders are fluid; the areas and lines are drawn roughly. Coast outlines: Natural Earth (public domain). As of November 2026.

satzmelodie.lead: Same words, a different melody: at the end of the sentence your voice goes down ↘ or up ↗. Listen, compare and repeat.

satzmelodie.note.some: {n} of {total} sentences have a recording. Your browser reads the others aloud.
satzmelodie.task1.title: Listen and compare the melody.
satzmelodie.task1.text: Repeat after me: after each sentence you have time to say it out loud. With the microphone 🎤 next to a sentence you can check your own melody – the recording stays on your device.
satzmelodie.caveat: Careful, echo question ↗↗: in Italian, “Marco viene domani?” and “Marco viene domani.” have the same words, so the melody is what makes it a question. A normal yes/no question rises a little. An echo question rises much higher, and it means something different: you're surprised or checking that you heard right (“Che viene domani?”).
satzmelodie.mic.title: Repeat and check
satzmelodie.task2.title: Listen. Statement, question or exclamation?
satzmelodie.task2.text: The words are always the same. Only the melody is different. Add the punctuation marks.
satzmelodie.task3.title: Which word is stressed? Click it.
satzmelodie.task3.text: The answer is always the same sentence. The question decides which word gets the stress.
satzmelodie.task4.title: Melody maze: which exit?
satzmelodie.task4.text: Quaki hops through the sentence with the voice. At the end the path splits: does the voice go up, down, or steeply down? Then you see the real melody – and Quaki rides along it.
satzmelodie.lab.aria: Maze: at the end of the sentence the path splits into three exits – top: question, bottom: statement, very bottom: exclamation.
satzmelodie.rule.title: The melody at the end of the sentence
satzmelodie.rule.aussage: The voice falls at the end.
satzmelodie.rule.w: The voice usually falls at the end, as in a statement. Questions with che cosa, dove, quando, chi, come, perché, quanto and quale. With a gentle rise instead, they sound extra friendly.
satzmelodie.rule.jn: Often the same words as a statement: only the melody, and ? in writing, makes it a question. The voice rises at the end.
satzmelodie.rule.echo: The voice rises high at the end. You're surprised or checking what you heard. Italian often starts it with che or davvero.
satzmelodie.rule.ausruf: The stressed word goes very high, then the voice falls a long way. Feeling: joy, anger, surprise.
satzmelodie.rule.liste: The voice stays level → until the list is finished. Then it falls ↘.
satzmelodie.teacherTip: For teachers: a pair activity with three cards (. ? !). A says “Marco viene domani” with one melody, B holds up the matching card.

satzmelodie.res.echoTip: In an echo question the voice goes up sharply at the end, even more clearly than in a yes/no question.
satzmelodie.res.endQuiet: The end of the sentence was too quiet to judge.

satzmelodie.why.ausruf: Exclamation: the voice starts high and falls sharply ↘. You're excited or surprised.

wissen.lernen.lead: Mistakes are allowed. Even more: without mistakes you learn more slowly. Here Bruno, Regi, Hamsti and Quaki explain how your brain really holds on to Italian.
wissen.lernen.jungle.title: Your brain is a jungle
wissen.lernen.jungle.lead: Imagine this: a new word lies on the other side of a dense jungle. There's no path to it yet. You have to cut it yourself.
wissen.lernen.jungle.machete.title: The machete
wissen.lernen.jungle.machete.text: Learning is your machete. On your first try you hack your way through the jungle with effort. That's tiring – and completely normal.
wissen.lernen.jungle.falsch.title: The wrong way
wissen.lernen.jungle.falsch.text: Sometimes you walk in the wrong direction: a mistake. Your brain notices the difference between what it expected and the right answer. That very signal shows it where the path really goes.
wissen.lernen.jungle.pfad.title: The beaten path
wissen.lernen.jungle.pfad.text: Every time you walk the path again, it gets wider. Nerve cells that often work together connect more strongly.
wissen.lernen.jungle.strasse.title: The road
wissen.lernen.jungle.strasse.text: After many repetitions the path has become a road. You don't have to think anymore – the word is just there. Practice even changes the wiring in your brain along the way.
wissen.lernen.jungle.foot1: And a path you don't walk for a long time? It slowly grows over again. That's why you repeat (Rule 3).
wissen.lernen.jungle.foot2: Your brain constantly rebuilding itself like this is called neuroplasticity. Adults who learn to juggle for three months have measurably more grey matter afterwards
wissen.lernen.jungle.foot4: And London taxi drivers, who learn thousands of streets, have a changed hippocampus
wissen.lernen.jungle.foot5: Your brain learns at any age.
wissen.lernen.wheel.label: The seven rules
wissen.lernen.wheel.title: The learning circle
wissen.lernen.rule.fehler.title: Making mistakes is part of it
wissen.lernen.rule.fehler.text: You're not supposed to get everything right straight away. If you try an answer, get it wrong and then see the right one, you remember it better than if you only read it.
wissen.lernen.rule.fehler.why: A mistake surprises your brain. That surprise makes the correction stick. Even mistakes you were completely sure about get corrected especially well afterwards. The only important thing: always look at the right answer.
wissen.lernen.rule.erinnern.say: Hmm … what was it called again?
wissen.lernen.rule.erinnern.title: Recall first, then check
wissen.lernen.rule.erinnern.text: Reading a word list five times feels good – but doesn't do much. Better: cover the word and quiz yourself. Only then do you check.
wissen.lernen.rule.erinnern.why: Every time you pull a word out of your head, the path to it gets wider. Reading only goes through your eyes. Remembering is work, and that very work is what stays.
wissen.lernen.rule.oft.title: A little, but often – and sleep well
wissen.lernen.rule.oft.text: Ten minutes every day are better than two hours on Sunday. And when you've almost forgotten a word, that's the best moment to review it.
wissen.lernen.rule.oft.why: With breaks between reviews, knowledge stays much longer. While you sleep, your brain sorts what you learned during the day. So learning in the evening and a quick review in the morning go well together.
wissen.lernen.rule.mischen.title: Mix instead of blocks
wissen.lernen.rule.mischen.text: Twenty sentences with only the present tense are easy – you already know what's coming. In real life you don't. So mix it up: present, passato prossimo and imperfetto, all jumbled.
wissen.lernen.rule.mischen.why: When you mix, you learn not only the rule but also when you need it. That's harder, but it's exactly what you need in conversation and in the exam.
wissen.lernen.rule.laut.title: Speak out loud, don't just read
wissen.lernen.rule.laut.text: Read new sentences out loud. Speak along when you listen to audio. Even alone in the kitchen – that's not weird, that's training.
wissen.lernen.rule.laut.why: What you say out loud, you also hear, and you move your mouth while doing it. So your head remembers the sentence in several ways. And your mouth learns the words before you need them in a conversation.
wissen.lernen.rule.schwer.title: It can be hard – but not too hard
wissen.lernen.rule.schwer.text: If everything is easy, you learn little. If everything is too hard, you give up. You learn the most in between: you have to think, but you usually manage.
wissen.lernen.rule.schwer.why: The effort isn't a sign that you're bad at it. It's the sign that you're learning right now. Choose your level so that you get about eight out of ten tasks right.
wissen.lernen.rule.feiern.title: Celebrate small steps
wissen.lernen.rule.feiern.text: Don't compare yourself with others. Compare yourself with yourself a month ago. Every new word is a step.
wissen.lernen.rule.feiern.why: Anyone who sees their progress keeps learning. Small goals that you really reach keep you going longer than one big goal that's far away.
wissen.lernen.sum.title: In short
wissen.lernen.sum.1: Try it yourself first – even if you get it wrong.
wissen.lernen.sum.2: After every mistake, look at the right answer.
wissen.lernen.sum.3: Better a little every day than a lot once.
wissen.lernen.sum.4: Mix the topics and speak out loud.
wissen.lernen.studies.title: The studies
wissen.lernen.studies.lead: The asterisks (*) in the text lead here. The studies are in English.
wissen.lernen.study.schultz: The brain signals the difference between expectation and outcome – this error signal steers learning.
wissen.lernen.study.rumelhart: Artificial neural networks learn by correcting their connections a little after every error.
wissen.lernen.study.hebb: Nerve cells that are often active at the same time connect more strongly – the basic idea behind the “beaten path”.
wissen.lernen.study.bengtsson: A lot of practice changes the nerve pathways themselves (the white matter).
wissen.lernen.study.draganski: After three months of juggling, adults' grey matter grew – and shrank back when they stopped.
wissen.lernen.study.boyke: The same works for people around 60, too.
wissen.lernen.study.maguire: London taxi drivers, who learn thousands of streets, have a changed hippocampus – the longer in the job, the clearer it is.
wissen.lernen.study.kornell: Guessing wrong first and then seeing the answer helps more than reading the answer straight away.
wissen.lernen.study.butterfield: Mistakes you were sure about are remembered especially well after they are corrected.
wissen.lernen.study.metcalfe: Overview: mistakes that get corrected help learning instead of harming it.
wissen.lernen.study.roediger: Quizzing yourself keeps knowledge longer than reading it again.
wissen.lernen.study.cepeda: Reviewing with breaks in between beats learning in one go.
wissen.lernen.study.rasch: During sleep the brain consolidates what was learned during the day.
wissen.lernen.study.rohrer: Mixed tasks did clearly better in the later test than tasks in blocks.
wissen.lernen.study.macleod: Words read aloud are remembered better than words read silently.
wissen.lernen.study.bjork: “Desirable difficulties”: what feels hard while practising often stays longer.
wissen.lernen.study.wilson: Learning models make the fastest progress when they get about 85% of the tasks right.
